name: Ascorbyl glucoside

lead: Ascorbyl glucoside is vitamin C with a glucose unit attached, which keeps it stable in skincare formulas. People use it in serums and creams for brighter skin, more even tone and fewer visible pigment marks.

It is described as a precursor that releases ascorbic acid in the skin, where vitamin C acts as an antioxidant and reduces melanin production. A small case series used an ascorbyl glucoside preparation with iontophoresis in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and it appears among whitening ingredients in cosmetic analysis papers; its rate of conversion to ascorbic acid is unknown.

paras: It is applied daily as a leave-on serum or cream, often in the morning under sunscreen and paired with other brightening ingredients such as niacinamide. Skincare communities treat it as a gentler, more stable alternative to pure ascorbic acid. Visible brightening is typically judged over weeks.
No specific safety problems are described in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, and like any topical it can be tolerated differently from person to person.

angle.text: Ascorbyl glucoside is a stabilised vitamin C derivative used in serums to brighten skin, even tone and slow visible ageing, by delivering antioxidant vitamin C and reducing melanin production. Research specific to this derivative is small.

lead: Ascorbyl glucoside is a form of vitamin C built for skincare. People use serums and creams containing it to brighten a dull complexion, even out dark spots and post-acne marks, and give skin a more uniform tone, using it as a stable, easy-to-formulate alternative to straight ascorbic acid.

Ascorbyl glucoside (also written AA-2G; chemical name L-ascorbic acid 2-O-alpha-glucoside) is a derivative of ascorbic acid in which a glucose unit is attached to the vitamin C molecule. It is commonly used in cosmetic products as a way of delivering vitamin C to the skin.

In skincare it is marketed for brightening, evening skin tone and reducing the look of pigmentation, and it appears in cosmetic analytical studies alongside other whitening ingredients such as kojic acid and niacinamide [1][2]. Skincare communities discuss it as a gentler or more stable alternative to pure ascorbic acid.

Evidence specific to ascorbyl glucoside is limited. One small uncontrolled study in melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation used a proprietary ascorbyl glucoside preparation combined with a device and acid regimen, which makes it hard to attribute any effect to the ingredient alone [3]. Wikipedia notes that clinical efficacy data for its use in skin whitening are not given in its source material, and that its rate of conversion to ascorbic acid in the body is unknown.

paras: Ascorbyl glucoside is an ascorbic acid derivative containing a glycosyl group; related ascorbyl glucosides have also shown antiscorbutic (anti-scurvy) activity. The molecular formula is C12H18O11 and it is produced through reactions catalysed by glycosyltransferase-class enzymes.

Glycosylated forms of ascorbic acid are described in the nutrition literature as products of in vitro transglycosidation rather than compounds found in nature, unlike glycosides of several other vitamins [4].

Wikipedia traces the earliest dated work on the compound it cites to a November 1990 study of its antiscorbutic (anti-scurvy) activity in rats and guinea pigs. Its registry identifiers include CAS 129499-78-1 and PubChem CID 54693473. Chemically it is a 2-O-alpha-glucoside: the glucose group sits on the same position of the ring that is normally vulnerable to oxidation, which is the design logic behind the derivative.

Plain ascorbic acid is described as a powerful antioxidant with potential skin benefits, but its topical use is limited by instability in conventional formulations [5]. Derivatives such as ascorbyl glucoside are used as an alternative form; Wikipedia says it has been credited with superior stability and penetration compared with ascorbyl phosphate salts.
Analytical chemistry papers have developed methods for measuring ascorbyl glucoside in skin-whitening and bleaching cosmetics, indicating its presence in commercial lightening products [1][2][6].

sections.h: Why vitamin C is used on skin
paras: Vitamin C is a cofactor for the hydroxylase enzymes that build the collagen triple helix, and it neutralises reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and can regenerate other antioxidants such as alpha-tocopherol [7]. These are the biochemical reasons it is promoted for firmness, photo-damage and tone. The same page describes ascorbic acid as one of the most labile vitamins, with oxidation accelerated by light, oxygen, heat, higher pH and metal salts [7]. That instability is why cosmetic chemists use derivatives such as ascorbyl glucoside, ascorbyl palmitate and ascorbyl phosphate salts, and why skincare users look for opaque packaging and 'stable' vitamin C labels.

Skincare communities discuss ascorbyl glucoside as a gentler and more stable alternative to pure ascorbic acid; the published trial evidence is described below. Wikipedia states that the in vivo conversion rate to ascorbic acid is unknown, which is the open question behind how much active vitamin C a skin cell receives.

A 2013 study in 35 patients (34 women, 1 man) with melasma or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation used a full-face iontophoresis mask with a proprietary vitamin C (ascorbyl glucoside) preparation, alongside a mandelic/malic acid regimen [3]. It was a combined-treatment study without a comparison group on the ingredient alone.
A 2024 Bayesian network meta-analysis compared 14 molecules for inhibiting UV daylight-induced pigmentation; it addresses topical depigmenting agents as a class [8].
No randomised controlled trial testing ascorbyl glucoside alone against placebo for appearance outcomes was identified.

Wikipedia's article on the compound contains no safety or toxicology section. Formal irritation data specific to ascorbyl glucoside are not part of the published studies cited here. Regulatory treatment of cosmetic ingredients varies by region, and ascorbyl glucoside is sold in over-the-counter cosmetics rather than as a drug.
